idea_html:
Keep two structures per item and let them disagree on purpose. A dict bids[item][user] = amount is the truth. A max-heap of (-amount, -userId) per item is only an index: every add and update pushes a new entry and never removes the old one; remove deletes from the dict only. getHighestBidder looks at the heap top and asks the dict whether that user still bids exactly that amount. If not, the entry is stale: pop it and look again. Ties go to the larger userId because the second key is -userId.

Sample 1: addBid(1,7,5), addBid(2,7,6): dict {1:5, 2:6}, heap top (-6,-2) matches, query returns 2. updateBid(1,7,8) pushes (-8,-1), dict {1:8, 2:6}; top (-8,-1) matches, returns 1. removeBid(2,7) deletes user 2 from the dict; the (-6,-2) entry stays in the heap but is not on top, so the query still returns 1. Item 3 has no dict entry: -1. Output [null,null,null,2,null,1,null,1,-1].

Each call is O(log m), m = pushes so far on that item; every stale entry is popped at most once, so 5·104 calls cost O(5·104 log) in total. Space O(total calls). The ordered-set variant (C++ std::set, Java TreeSet) deletes the old entry eagerly and gives the same bound without amortization.
pitfalls_html:
• Scan the item's dict on every query. Add, update and remove are O(1) but getHighestBidder is O(bidders). Total calls are capped at 5·104, so the worst split is 25,000 addBid on one item followed by 25,000 queries: 6.25·108 dict visits. Measured locally on exactly that input: 13.0 s in Python, 3.2 s in Java. On LeetCode three such submissions (Python, Java, JavaScript) timed out at test 498–499 of 509.
  • Tie-break in the wrong direction. A comparator "amount descending, then userId ascending" read with first(), or a Python heap keyed (-amount, userId), returns the smallest userId on equal bids. Input: addBid(3,7,8), addBid(5,7,8), getHighestBidder(7) expects 5; the reversed order returns 3. One Java submission with exactly this comparator failed at test 503 of 509.
  • Lazy heap that only checks "user still has a bid". After a bid is lowered, the old higher entry is still in the heap and the user is still in the dict, so the stale entry wins. Input: addBid(1,7,10), addBid(2,7,6), updateBid(1,7,3), getHighestBidder(7) expects 2; the presence-only check returns 1. Compare the amount too.
  • Delete from a Python heap with list.remove then heapify. Both are O(n) per call. 25,000 bids on one item then 25,000 updates, each removing its old entry: measured 24.6 s locally. (A plain sorted list with bisect.insort is O(n) per insert on paper but the shift is one memmove: 50,000 adversarial inserts took 0.20 s, so that approach does not time out at this size.)

Sorted list with bisect.insort 'TLE' is false at this size: 50,000 adversarial inserts took 0.20 s locally (the shift is a memmove). Item dropped; noted inside pitfall 4.
heap.remove: '5e4 * 5e4 = 2.5e9 ops' repeats the cap error; worst case is 25,000 x 25,000 = 6.25e8 per O(n) step. TLE verdict kept (24.6 s measured).
Essence: 'a sorted structure inverts this' (O(n) add, O(1) max) describes a sorted array, not an ordered set, which gives O(log n) for both. Rewritten.
